blocks.text: We can use E° values to calculate the voltage of an electrochemical cell made up of two half-cells, even when neither of them is a standard hydrogen electrode. The voltage measured is the difference between the E° values of the two half-cells. we call this value the standard cell potential (E°Cell).
For the electrochemical cell shown in Figure 10.8 (a), the two relevant half-equations are:
The voltage of this cell is +0.80 – (–0.76) = +1.56 V as in Figure 10.8 (b).

blocks.alt: (a) Two half-cells joined by a salt bridge at 298 K: a silver rod marked Ag in Ag+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal +, and a zinc rod marked Zn in Zn2+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal -, wired to a voltmeter reading 1.56 V; arrows on the wire run from zinc to silver, e- marked at both ends. (b) An E-standard scale from +1.00 to -1.00 with Ag+ + e- in equilibrium with Ag at +0.80 V (red) and Zn2+ + 2e- in equilibrium with Zn at -0.76 V (blue), joined by a double arrow marked 1.56 V.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.8: (a) An Ag+/Ag, Zn2+/Zn electrochemical cell, (b) The difference between +0.80 V and -0.76 V is +1.56 V (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 10.8 (a) draws the e⁻ arrows on the wire from silver (+) to zinc (–); electrons flow from zinc to silver, as drawn above. In (b) the two half-equations are placed at their true positions, +0.80 V and –0.76 V.

blocks.title: Quick Check 10.7
blocks.text:
i) What is the function of salt bridge in the voltaic cell?
ii) Calculate the voltage of a cell having iron and copper electrodes.
Fe(s) ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ E° = – 0.44 V
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s) E° = – 0.44 V

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book gives E° = – 0.44 V for Cu²⁺/Cu here, repeating the value for iron. The E° of Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V (Figure 10.9), so the iron-copper cell gives +0.34 – (–0.44) = +0.78 V.
The E° value for the Ag⁺/Ag half-cell is more positive than for the Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell. So, the Ag⁺/Ag half-cell is the positive pole and the Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell is the negative pole of the cell.
